A dashboard/CSV/PDF example found in one report was dropped: it is unclear it is Fitzpatrick's own account. Old text's three 'mistakes' and invented quotes dropped.
facts: Chapter on bad data names three kinds: compliments, fluff and ideas.
'Compliments are the fool's gold of customer learning: shiny, distracting, and worthless.'
To handle a compliment, do not accept it; ask why they like it, what else they have tried, what it cost them.
Fluff has three forms: generic claims ('I usually', 'I always'), future promises ('I will', 'I would') and hypotheticals ('I might', 'I could').
The most dangerous line is 'I would definitely buy that'; steer back to the last time they ran into the problem.
When someone asks for a feature, find the problem under it: 'Why do you want that?'
scene_details: the last time they ran into the problem
tension: The warmest, most promising things a customer says are the least useful.
opening_idea: Open on 'I would definitely buy that', the sentence the book calls the most dangerous kind of fluff.

lessons.idea: Treat praise and promises as noise until a specific past example backs them.
lessons.anchor: fool's gold compliments and 'I would definitely buy that'.
lessons.example: A friend says they would love your recipe box; asking when they last cooked from scratch tells you more.

reflect_final: What was the last compliment or promise about your work that you took as good news, and what specific question could have tested it?

use_cases.situation: Someone says 'that is a great idea' after you describe your plan.
use_cases.move: Thank them and ask what they do today about the problem and when it last cost them time or money; the book calls compliments fool's gold.

use_cases.situation: A customer says they would definitely buy it when it is ready.
use_cases.move: Ask them to walk through the last time the problem came up and what they tried; that is how the book turns 'I would' into evidence.

use_cases.situation: A user asks for a new feature.
use_cases.move: Before you add a requested feature, ask 'Why do you want that?' and what they do about it now; the book treats a feature request as a symptom of a deeper problem.

pocket_idea: Compliments and 'I would buy that' are fool's gold: ask what they did the last time the problem came up.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A compliment feels like a result but it has no facts in it.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: A customer asked Fitzpatrick for analytics, so he built a flexible dashboard. Then came CSV export, then PDFs. They only wanted good-looking charts to show their own clients each week. Asking why behind the request would have saved the build.
